secondary_sources.title: Thomas Mofolo and the Emergence of Written Sesotho Prose

contested_points: Published birth years cluster around 1876 but mission registers and later biographies do not always agree on the exact day.
Mission authorities delayed and revised publication of Chaka; scholars debate how far theological censorship shaped the final text.
Readers disagree on how much oral tradition versus authorial invention drives the psychology of Chaka in the novel.
known_myths: Chaka is literary fiction, not a verbatim transcript of nineteenth-century Zulu history or eyewitness testimony.
Thomas Mofolo did not meet Shaka kaSenzangakhona; Shaka died decades before Mofolo was born.
Social media sometimes attributes modern motivational quotes to Mofolo without a published Sesotho or French source.

retrieval_cards.text: Chaka is a Sesotho novel published in 1925 that reimagines the rise of Shaka through literary prose; historians treat it as imaginative literature that influenced later African writing.
Moeti oa Bochabela (1907) is widely cited as among the earliest sustained novels in Sesotho, blending moral journey with mission-era Basutoland settings.
Biographical studies place Mofolo in Basutoland mission networks, including clerical and translation work for the Paris Evangelical Mission Society before his major novels.
Pitseng (1910) is a Sesotho love story set in mission-influenced society; it shows Mofolo's range beyond the Chaka epic.
Reference histories of African literature classify Mofolo as a pioneer of written Sesotho prose while warning that Chaka must not be read as neutral documentary history.
The novel's Shaka is a tragic literary figure shaped by prophecy, power, and isolation; language quests may discuss themes only with legend or inference labels when sources disagree.
Standard biographies record Thomas Mofolo's death on 8 September 1948 in Basutoland; learners should refuse knowledge after that date.
